questions.stem: Which list gives Earth's layers in order from the centre outwards?
options: Solid metallic inner core, silicate outer core, liquid metallic mantle, crust
Solid metallic inner core, liquid metallic outer core, silicate mantle, crust
Liquid metallic inner core, solid metallic outer core, silicate mantle, crust
Solid silicate inner core, liquid metallic outer core, metallic mantle, crust
questions.explanation: Earth has a solid iron-nickel inner core, a liquid iron-nickel outer core, a thick silicate mantle and a thin silicate crust.

questions.stem: How did Earth come to have a dense metallic core beneath a silicate mantle and crust?
options: The core formed first as a separate body and later captured a silicate shell from space
While early Earth was largely molten, dense iron and nickel sank and lighter silicates rose
Iron meteorites struck Earth late in its history and were buried deep beneath the crust and mantle
Silicate rock was slowly converted into iron by the heat and pressure deep inside Earth
questions.explanation: Earth internally differentiated. Heat from impacts and radioactive decay melted much of the early planet, letting dense metal sink to the centre while less dense silicate material formed the mantle and crust.

questions.stem: Which property of seismic waves is used to show that Earth's outer core is liquid?
options: Surface waves travel only through liquids, not solids
Neither P nor S waves can travel through any liquid
S waves cannot travel through liquids, but P waves can
P waves cannot travel through liquids, but S waves can
questions.explanation: S waves are shear waves and need a rigid material to travel through. P waves are compressional and pass through solids, liquids and gases.

questions.stem: After a large earthquake, no direct S waves are recorded at stations more than about 103° from the epicentre. What does this S-wave shadow zone show?
options: Seismometers far from earthquakes are too sensitive to record S waves
A liquid layer, the outer core, blocks S waves deep inside Earth
The mantle is liquid, so S waves cannot pass through any of it
The inner core is hollow, so S waves bounce straight back up
questions.explanation: S waves travelling deep enough to reach the core are stopped because the outer core is liquid, leaving a large region on the far side of Earth with no direct S waves.

questions.stem: Between about 103° and 142° from an earthquake there is a P-wave shadow zone, but faint P waves are still recorded within it. What did these faint P waves reveal?
options: A hollow centre that lets P waves travel straight through without bending
A second crust beneath the mantle that sends P waves back to the surface
A solid inner core that bends and reflects P waves into the shadow zone
A liquid mantle that slows P waves until they stop inside the shadow zone
questions.explanation: The main shadow zone forms because P waves are refracted where they enter the liquid outer core. Weak arrivals inside it are explained by a boundary deeper inside, a solid inner core, which was first proposed by Inge Lehmann.

questions.stem: Seismic waves speed up sharply at a depth of about 5 to 70 km beneath the surface. What does this boundary, the Moho, mark?
options: The change from liquid outer core to solid inner core
The change from mantle to liquid outer core below it
The change from oceanic crust to continental crust
The change from crust to denser mantle rock beneath
questions.explanation: Seismic waves travel faster in denser, more rigid rock. The jump in speed at the Moho shows the crust lies on denser mantle rock. Its depth varies because continental crust is much thicker than oceanic crust.

questions.stem: Why are meteorites used as evidence for the composition of Earth's interior?
options: Meteorites contain trapped seismic waves that record the structure of the early Earth
Iron meteorites resemble the core and stony meteorites the mantle of differentiated bodies
Meteorites are pieces of Earth's core blasted into space by ancient volcanic eruptions
Meteorites are made of the same rock as Earth's crust, so they show the crust's thickness
questions.explanation: Meteorites are fragments of early solar system bodies, some of which differentiated like Earth. Iron-nickel meteorites match the composition inferred for the core, and stony meteorites resemble mantle material.

questions.stem: Earth's average density is about 5.5 g/cm³, but rocks of the crust have densities of only about 2.7 to 3.0 g/cm³. What does this indicate?
options: The crust must be the densest layer, since it is under the greatest pressure of any layer
The average density must be wrong, since all of Earth is made of crustal rock
The interior must contain material much denser than crustal rock, such as iron
The interior must be largely hollow, which lowers Earth's overall density
questions.explanation: If the outer layers are less dense than the average, the inside must be denser to make up the difference. This supports a dense metallic core.

questions.stem: How does oceanic crust differ from continental crust?
options: Oceanic crust is thicker, less dense and granitic; continental crust is thinner, denser and basaltic
Oceanic crust is metallic and liquid; continental crust is silicate and solid
Oceanic crust and continental crust are identical except for the water above
Oceanic crust is thinner, denser and basaltic; continental crust is thicker, less dense and granitic
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is about 7 km thick and made of basalt and gabbro. Continental crust is typically 30 to 70 km thick and has an overall granitic composition, which makes it less dense.

questions.stem: A geology student is asked how the terms mineral and rock are related. Which answer is correct?
options: Minerals are composed of one or more rocks
Rocks and minerals are two names for the same thing
Minerals form only after rocks have been melted
Rocks are composed of one or more minerals
questions.explanation: A mineral is a naturally occurring inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and ordered crystal structure. Rocks are aggregates of one or more minerals.

questions.stem: When identifying a mineral sample, what does its streak refer to?
options: The colour of its powder, seen by rubbing it on an unglazed porcelain plate
The colour of the mineral's outer surface when it is held up to bright light
The pattern of flat surfaces left when the mineral is broken with a hammer
The scratch the mineral leaves when it is rubbed against a piece of glass
questions.explanation: Streak is the colour of the finely powdered mineral. It is more reliable than surface colour, which can vary with impurities and weathering.

questions.stem: A sample of hematite is shiny and steel-grey, yet it leaves a red-brown mark on a streak plate. Why is streak more useful than colour for identifying it?
options: Streak is consistent for a mineral, while its surface colour can vary
Streak changes with each sample, so it records where the mineral formed
Colour is always the same for every mineral, so it cannot tell them apart
Streak shows how hard the mineral is, which colour cannot show at all
questions.explanation: Hematite can be grey, black or red in hand specimen, but its powder is always red-brown. Many minerals vary in colour, so streak is the more diagnostic property.

questions.stem: A mineral scratches glass but is scratched by quartz. Which Mohs hardness value fits?
questions.explanation: Glass has a hardness of about 5.5 and quartz is 7, so the mineral lies between them. Orthoclase feldspar, hardness 6, is an example.

questions.stem: Which list of minerals is in order of increasing hardness on the Mohs scale?
options: Quartz, talc, diamond, calcite
Calcite, diamond, talc, quartz
Talc, calcite, quartz, diamond
Diamond, quartz, calcite, talc
questions.explanation: On the Mohs scale talc is 1, calcite 3, quartz 7 and diamond 10. The scale is relative, ranking minerals by which can scratch which.

questions.stem: Mica splits easily into thin, flat sheets, but quartz breaks along curved, shell-like surfaces. Which statement is correct?
options: Mica has one direction of cleavage; quartz shows conchoidal fracture
Mica shows conchoidal fracture; quartz has one direction of cleavage
Both minerals show cleavage, but mica's is curved and quartz's is flat
Both minerals show fracture, because neither breaks along flat planes
questions.explanation: Cleavage is breakage along flat planes of weakness in the crystal structure. Fracture is irregular breakage; quartz has no cleavage and breaks with curved conchoidal surfaces like glass.

questions.stem: Halite (rock salt) always breaks into small cubes. What does this show about its cleavage?
options: It has three directions of cleavage at right angles
It has one direction of cleavage parallel to its base
It has no cleavage and breaks by conchoidal fracture
It has two directions of cleavage at about 60 degrees
questions.explanation: Three cleavage planes meeting at 90° produce cubic fragments. Calcite also has three cleavage directions, but they are not at right angles, so it breaks into rhombs.

questions.stem: The lustre of a mineral describes:
options: the colour of its powder when rubbed on an unglazed porcelain plate
how easily it can be scratched by other minerals or common objects
how much heavier it feels than an equal volume of water or quartz
the way its surface reflects light, such as metallic, glassy or earthy
questions.explanation: Lustre is the appearance of a mineral's surface in reflected light. Metallic lustre looks like polished metal; non-metallic lustres include vitreous (glassy), pearly and earthy.

questions.stem: Several dark grey, metallic-looking minerals look similar in hand specimen. One is strongly attracted to a magnet. Which mineral is it, most likely?
options: Magnetite
Hematite
Graphite
Molybdenite
questions.explanation: Magnetite is the only common mineral that is strongly magnetic. Hematite is also an iron oxide but is not noticeably magnetic and has a red-brown streak, and graphite and molybdenite are soft and non-magnetic.

questions.stem: A mineral has a metallic grey lustre, a grey streak, breaks into cubes and feels very heavy for its size. Which mineral is it?
options: Magnetite
Galena
Pyrite
Graphite
questions.explanation: Galena, lead sulfide, is grey and metallic with cubic cleavage and a very high density. Pyrite is brassy yellow with a greenish-black streak, graphite is soft and greasy, and magnetite is magnetic with no cleavage.

questions.stem: How do igneous rocks form?
options: By heat and pressure changing rock without melting
By weathering of rocks at Earth's surface into soil
By cooling and crystallisation of magma or lava
By compaction and cementation of sediment layers
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks crystallise from molten rock, either slowly underground or rapidly at the surface. Compaction and cementation form sedimentary rocks, and solid-state change forms metamorphic rocks.

questions.stem: Which sequence of processes forms a sedimentary rock from an older rock?
options: Deposition, weathering, melting, then compaction of the melted grains
Compaction, cementation, weathering, then deposition of the cement
Weathering, erosion and transport, deposition, compaction and cementation
Melting, cooling, crystallisation, then weathering of the cooled lava
questions.explanation: Rocks are broken down by weathering, the fragments are eroded and carried away, then deposited in layers. Burial compacts the sediment and minerals cement the grains together, a process called lithification.

questions.stem: How do metamorphic rocks form?
options: Molten rock cools quickly at the surface so that the crystals have little or no time to grow
Sediment is buried and cemented by minerals carried in circulating groundwater
Weathering at the surface breaks rock into fragments that are carried by rivers
Heat and pressure change the minerals and texture of a rock while it remains solid
questions.explanation: Metamorphism happens in the solid state. Minerals recrystallise or new minerals grow under higher temperature and pressure; if the rock melted, it would form magma instead.

questions.stem: Granite on a hillside weathers to quartz sand, which is carried to a beach. Much later the sand has become quartzite. Which sequence of rock cycle processes occurred?
options: Weathering and erosion, deposition and lithification, then metamorphism
Melting and crystallisation, then weathering, then cementation only
Metamorphism, then melting, then deposition and lithification of the melt
Deposition, then melting, then weathering and lithification
questions.explanation: Weathering and erosion freed the quartz grains, which were deposited and lithified into sandstone. Heat and pressure then recrystallised the sandstone into quartzite. Any rock can become another type through the rock cycle.

questions.stem: Graded bedding is a layer in which:
options: grain size changes from fine at the base to coarse at the top
all the grains are the same size throughout the whole layer
thin layers are inclined at an angle to the main bedding
grain size changes from coarse at the base to fine at the top
questions.explanation: Graded beds form when a current slows down, so the coarsest grains settle first and progressively finer grains follow. Turbidity currents on the sea floor commonly produce them.

questions.stem: Cross-bedding consists of sets of inclined layers within a sandstone bed. How does it form?
options: Sand is folded by tectonic forces after it has turned into sandstone
Sand is deposited on the downstream face of migrating ripples or dunes
Sand settles slowly from still water, forming layers that slope gently
Sand cracks as it dries in the sun, and the cracks fill with new sand
questions.explanation: As wind or water moves sand over a ripple or dune, grains avalanche down its front face, building inclined layers. Cross-bedding shows a current was present and which way it flowed.

questions.stem: Mud cracks are preserved in many successive layers of a mudstone sequence. Which environment does this best indicate?
options: A deep ocean floor that remained covered by thousands of metres of water
A fast-flowing mountain river that carried boulders along its channel
A thick glacier that ground across the land without ever melting
A lake margin or floodplain that was repeatedly flooded and then dried out
questions.explanation: Mud cracks form when wet mud dries and shrinks, so they show periods of exposure to air. Repeated cracked layers record repeated wetting and drying, typical of lake margins, floodplains and tidal flats.

questions.stem: A steeply tilted sandstone bed has coarse grains at the top of the bed and fine grains at the bottom, as it is now seen in an outcrop. What can be concluded?
options: The bed has been overturned, because graded beds fine upwards when deposited
The bed is the right way up, because coarse grains always settle last
The bed was deposited by wind, because wind always deposits the coarse grains on top
The bed tells nothing about its orientation, because grading is random
questions.explanation: Graded bedding is a way-up indicator: when deposited, beds fine upwards. Finding the coarse grains at the top shows the bed has been turned upside down by folding.

questions.stem: A sandstone contains cross-beds several metres high. Its grains are well sorted, well rounded and frosted, and it has no marine fossils. Which environment does this indicate?
options: A glacier depositing mixed debris
Desert sand dunes built by wind
A deep, quiet lake bed with mud
A coral reef in a warm, clear sea
questions.explanation: Very large cross-beds form in wind-blown dunes, and wind transport rounds and frosts sand grains and sorts them well. Glaciers deposit poorly sorted debris and reefs form limestone.

questions.stem: In a cross-bedded sandstone, the inclined layers all dip towards the east. What does this show about the ancient current?
options: It flowed towards the west
It flowed straight up and down
It had no fixed direction
It flowed towards the east
questions.explanation: Cross-beds build on the downstream face of ripples and dunes, so they dip in the direction the current was flowing.

questions.stem: How do conglomerate and breccia differ?
options: Both have gravel-sized clasts, but conglomerate's are rounded and breccia's are angular
Both have sand-sized grains, but conglomerate's are angular and breccia's are rounded
Conglomerate is made of calcium carbonate, while breccia is made only of quartz sand grains
Conglomerate is a metamorphic rock, while breccia is an igneous rock from lava
questions.explanation: Both are coarse clastic rocks with fragments larger than 2 mm. Rounding of the clasts shows how far they travelled: rounded clasts in conglomerate, angular ones in breccia.

questions.stem: A breccia contains angular fragments of the rock that forms a nearby cliff. What does the angular shape of the fragments suggest?
options: They crystallised from magma that intruded the rocks beneath the cliff
They were transported only a short distance, such as in scree below the cliff
They were carried hundreds of kilometres by a large river before deposition
They were rolled for a long time on a beach by waves until they were smooth
questions.explanation: Transport by water rounds off sharp edges. Angular clasts have barely moved from their source, as in scree slopes, fault zones or landslide deposits.

questions.stem: A pale rock fizzes when dilute hydrochloric acid is dropped on it and contains many shell fragments. Which rock is it, most likely?
options: Siltstone
Mudstone
Limestone
Sandstone
questions.explanation: Limestone is made mainly of calcium carbonate, which reacts with dilute acid to release carbon dioxide. Many limestones are built from shells and skeletons of marine organisms.

questions.stem: Shale and mudstone are both made of very fine clay-sized particles. How can they be told apart in a hand specimen?
options: Mudstone splits easily into thin layers, while shale breaks into blocky pieces
Shale fizzes in dilute acid, while mudstone shows no reaction at all to acid
Mudstone contains rounded pebbles, while shale contains only angular sand
Shale splits easily into thin layers, while mudstone breaks into blocky pieces
questions.explanation: Shale is fissile: it parts along closely spaced bedding planes. Mudstone has the same fine grain size but lacks this layering and breaks into blocks.

questions.stem: Which list of sedimentary rocks is in order from coarsest to finest grain size?
options: Siltstone, shale, conglomerate, sandstone
Conglomerate, sandstone, siltstone, shale
Shale, siltstone, sandstone, conglomerate
Sandstone, conglomerate, shale, siltstone
questions.explanation: Conglomerate has gravel-sized clasts over 2 mm, sandstone sand-sized grains, siltstone silt-sized grains and shale clay-sized particles.

questions.stem: A rock is made of rounded quartz grains about 0.5 mm across, all of similar size. It does not react with dilute acid. Which rock is it?
options: Sandstone
Siltstone
Limestone
Conglomerate
questions.explanation: Grains of 0.5 mm are sand-sized (1/16 to 2 mm), so this is a sandstone. Siltstone is finer, conglomerate coarser, and limestone would fizz in acid.

questions.stem: A rock sequence grades upward from conglomerate, to sandstone, to shale. What change in the depositional environment does this suggest?
options: The energy of the water fell over time, for example as a river slowed or sea level rose
The energy of the water rose over time, for example as a lake turned into a fast river
The climate became much drier over time, so wind replaced water as the transport agent
The sediment source changed from quartz to calcium carbonate over time in a reef
questions.explanation: Coarse gravel needs fast-flowing water, sand moderate energy and clay quiet water. An upward-fining sequence shows the energy at that spot decreased over time.

questions.stem: Which list best describes what soil is composed of?
options: Organic material only, formed from the decay of dead plants and animals
Water and dissolved gases trapped between the grains of solid bedrock
Rock and mineral particles, organic material, water, gases and living organisms
Rock and mineral particles only, broken down from bedrock by physical weathering
questions.explanation: Soil is a mixture of weathered mineral matter, organic material, water, air and organisms such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms.

questions.stem: Soil formation requires interaction between atmospheric, geological, hydrological and biotic processes. Which of these is a biotic process in soil formation?
options: Earthworms and microbes break down leaf litter into humus
Rainwater dissolves minerals from the underlying bedrock
Freezing water expands in cracks and splits rock apart
Wind carries fine dust onto the land from distant deserts
questions.explanation: Biotic processes involve living things, such as decomposition of organic matter and mixing of soil by animals and roots. Dissolving minerals and frost wedging are hydrological and geological processes.

questions.stem: Why do soils usually form faster in warm, wet climates than in cold, dry ones?
options: Chemical weathering and biological activity are faster with more warmth and water
Rock is always softer in warm climates, so it crumbles away without needing any weathering
Cold climates have more organisms, which slow the breakdown of the rock
Rain washes away all the weathered material, leaving only the fresh rock
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions speed up with temperature, water is needed for most chemical weathering, and organisms that decompose material and mix soil are more active in warm, moist conditions.

questions.stem: In a soil profile, the A horizon is usually darker than the B horizon below it. What is the main reason?
options: The A horizon contains more iron oxide washed down from the bedrock
The A horizon is made of unweathered parent rock that has not changed
The A horizon is always wetter, and wet soil is the only dark soil
The A horizon contains more organic matter (humus) from decaying plants
questions.explanation: Leaf litter and roots add organic matter mainly near the surface, and humus darkens the topsoil. The B horizon below gathers clay and minerals washed down from above, and the C horizon is weathered parent rock.
